2062: The analysis of variance addresses one attribute at a time, so that a single figure was required to establish which cultivar is superior overall. This was accomplished using the total quality scoring approach of Ismail et al. (2001), in which each attribute is scored, weighted for its importance, and the weighted scores summed. Kraggerud et al. (2012) subsequently examined whether such a score genuinely reflects overall quality and concluded that it does. Here every attribute on which the cultivars differed significantly was placed on a scale of 0 to 100, oriented so that 100 invariably denotes the superior outcome, then averaged within five groups and combined by weight: sensory 30%, nutritional 25, bioactive 20, mineral 15 and colour 10. The weights constitute a stated convention rather than a property of the data, and the index may be recomputed under any alternative set. The result is given in Table 4.94, and the score of every cultivar in every group appears in Table 4.96.

2071: The table below gives the five group scores and the composite score for every cultivar in every product, so that the standing of any entry may be read directly. The weights applied were sensory 30%, nutritional 25, bioactive 20, mineral 15 and colour 10.
2076: The weights above were assigned rather than computed, so the ranking was verified against a second set of weights derived from the data themselves. Principal component analysis was performed on the merit scores, and each attribute was then weighted by the sum, over the components with an eigenvalue of one or more, of its squared loading multiplied by the share of variance that component carries. This constitutes the customary procedure for assigning weights to a composite indicator without recourse to judgement. The two rankings corresponded closely, with a mean Spearman correlation of 0.952 and a minimum of 0.939, and the same cultivar ranked first in 3 of the 3 products, as Table 4.97 demonstrates. The ranking therefore proceeds from the data and not from the particular weights adopted. Principal component analysis is employed here solely to assign the weights; the components themselves cannot rank the cultivars for quality, since a component measures the direction of greatest variation and takes no account of whether a high or a low value is the more desirable.
